findings.finding: Removing the reserved-word rejection is correct consumer behavior. GNU Multiboot v1 explicitly says: "The ‘reserved’ field must be set to 0 by the boot loader and ignored by the operating system." Loader nonconformance does not justify OS rejection.

All meaningful-field protections remain: bounded module count and table span before descriptor reads; checked address arithmetic and 32-bit physical ceiling; nonempty forward payload range; complete usable-RAM coverage with reserved-map precedence; kernel/growth exclusion; module/module and module/metadata overlap rejection, including metadata discovered later; bounded, validated, owned names and reservations including NUL. The reserved word is not interpreted as a pointer or length.

The new regression compares nonzero reserved values 1, 0xfffffffc and u32::MAX against the zero baseline for module ranges, reservations and selected owned metadata, without payload reads. Existing source-drop, partial-frame pinning, free-refusal and allocator-exhaustion tests remain unchanged. Runtime execution was not performed.

Default positive probing now ignores reserved-word contents while retaining descriptor count, payload length/content, exact label and guest success-marker checks at both RAM sizes. Raw descriptor bytes and per-RAM observations are saved. Producer-zero checking remains an explicit opt-in, separate from OS compatibility.

The two reserved-policy flags can be supplied together; --expect-reserved-rejection silently takes precedence over --require-zero-reserved. Consider making them mutually exclusive to avoid an ambiguous diagnostic invocation.

upstream_source_check: Inspected saved GRUB 2.12 multiboot_mbi.c: the module loop assigns start, end and cmdline but not pad; the preceding memset covers the information header rather than the module table.

limitations: Static scoped approval only; no guest, trust, publication or release acceptance claimed.
